title: DMC3 HD virtual dispatch: a census, and the receivers that can be named

records.title: 10,274 virtual dispatch sites, and no statically known receiver among them
records.summary: Recording each call through a register base rather than only its displacement gives a census of 10,274 dispatch sites in place of the 3,410 distinct displacements known before. Of those, the number whose receiver object the walk can name as a static address is zero: the pattern of taking a global object's address and reading its first quadword never occurs. Receivers arrive as arguments or through pointers loaded from writable data, whose values are established at run time and are not in the image. That is a property of the programme rather than a shortfall of the walk, and it means whole-image devirtualisation by reading the file cannot be had.

locations.note: 10,274 calls through a register base with a slot-aligned displacement; none reaches a receiver object at a static address.

records.title: A call on `this` names its own class, and 19 resolve to a target
records.summary: One receiver is knowable without any analysis of what a pointer holds: `this`. The Microsoft x64 convention puts the first argument in rcx, so a load through rcx, or through a register a method copied rcx into at entry, is the object's vtable pointer. The enclosing method's own binding then says which vtable that is, and the displacement says which slot, so the target is read from the vtable rather than inferred. 105 sites dispatch on `this`, 98 of them inside a method the RTTI binds into a vtable, and 19 in a method bound into exactly one vtable, which is what makes the class unambiguous. Those 19 resolve to a class, a slot and a target function across 15 classes, among them CPlDante, CPlVergil and the CEm enemy family. The number is small because the walk gives up its register state at every trace root, so only dispatches reachable in straight-line flow from a method's entry keep the fact; block-level dataflow with merges is what would lift it.

records.title: Which registers survive a call is an ABI fact, not an assumption
records.summary: The walk previously gave up every register at a call, because which ones survive looked like a claim it had no right to make. It is not a claim: the Microsoft x64 convention names rax, rcx, rdx and r8 to r11 volatile and the rest preserved, and compiler-generated code follows it. Forgetting only the volatile registers is what lets a `this` pointer copied into a saved register at entry still be `this` after the method has called something, and it lifts recall everywhere the same state is used: indexed reads with a nameable base rise from 1,357 to 1,524, consistent array walks from 304 to 368, and recovered arrays from 178 to 190. A test pins both halves, that a base in rcx is lost across a call and a base in rbx is not.

locations.symbol: executable section walked under the calling convention
locations.note: Volatile registers rax, rcx, rdx and r8 to r11 given up at every call; the rest carried across.

records.title: Block dataflow lifts the analysis, and shows what was really limiting it
records.summary: The register analysis now runs as its own pass over the instructions the walk decoded, with a state per instruction and a meet at every join, where the meet keeps a fact only when every path into the point agrees on it. That replaces a single pass whose facts depended on the order the traces happened to run. The code graph is unchanged, which is the check that the walk itself was not disturbed: the same 7,389 functions, the same 7,381 complete walks, byte for byte. Indexed reads with a nameable base rise from 1,524 to 1,963, consistent array walks from 368 to 531, recovered arrays from 190 to 278, dispatches on `this` from 105 to 175 and resolved dispatches from 19 to 30. The earlier reading held that dataflow was what stood between 105 and the thousands of dispatches in bound methods. It lifted the figure by two thirds and the rest is not analysis at all: the method at RVA 0x2A9A0 reads a container out of a field of `this`, takes an element pointer out of that container, and dispatches on the element. Its contents are built at run time and are not in the file. Most dispatch sites are of that shape, so the ceiling of 2,487 displacements in single-vtable methods was never reachable by following `this`.

records.title: A call on a base subobject resolves through that subobject's vtable
records.summary: A load through the first argument at a non-zero offset is the vtable pointer of whatever sits there, because a subobject's vtable pointer is at its own offset zero. Reading the offset as well as the fact of the load takes dispatches on `this` from 175 to 352, of which 177 are on something inside the object rather than on the object. Where that offset is one the RTTI records for one of the class's own vtables, the receiver is a base subobject and the call goes into that vtable — not the class's primary one, which holds a different function at the same slot. The RTTI settles this without any constructor store, which matters because a derived class inherits its layout from a base whose constructor did the storing: the classes doing these dispatches, CEm025 and CEm002 among them, are not the classes whose constructors write the vtables. Resolved dispatches rise from 30 to 47, 17 of them through a subobject. The method at RVA 0x116900 shows the whole form: it loads the vtable at this plus 96, passes this plus 96 as the receiver's own first argument, and calls slot 29 out of it.

records.title: Most calls on something inside the object go through a pointer, not a subobject
records.summary: A load out of the object at a non-zero offset was read as the vtable pointer of whatever sits there, which is right for an embedded subobject and wrong for a pointer. Counting how many loads deep the value is separates them: of 1,134 dispatches in the `this` family, 352 read the vtable straight out of the object and 782 read it through a pointer the object holds. 485 of those 782 go through one offset, 224, which is a pointer at a fixed place in a widely shared base. A pointer member's vtable is the pointee's, and the enclosing class's layout describes the pointer rather than the object, so these are counted and left alone rather than resolved against the wrong class. The distinction was very nearly lost: the field carrying the depth was written into the wrong slot of an aggregate initialiser, which set the multiplier instead and reported all 782 as direct subobject loads. The constructions now name their fields.

locations.symbol: executable section carrying the dispatch sites
locations.note: 1,134 dispatches on the object or something inside it: 352 at one load deep, 782 at two, of which 485 at offset 224.

records.title: What a constructor stores in a pointer field is memory, not yet an object
records.summary: Typing a pointer field looked like a short step: follow the value a call returned into the store that puts it in the object, and the callee names the type. 183 such stores exist, and not one callee is a constructor. The most common by far, at RVA 0x2E7CA0 with 86 of them, is an allocator: a small function bound into no vtable and constructing nothing. The object's class is established by the constructor that runs on that memory afterwards, between the allocation and the store, so typing the field needs that call followed too. Recording the stores and saying plainly that none of them types anything is worth more than a number that assumed the callee was a constructor.

locations.symbol: allocator whose result is stored into objects
locations.note: RVA 0x2E7CA0, the callee of 86 of the 183 stores of a returned value into the first argument; bound into no vtable and storing none.
